detail.longDescription: arXiv:2611.21977v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Socially assistive robots could expand access to group-based mental health support when skilled human facilitators are unavailable. However, their effectiveness will depend on whether they foster productive interactions among participants. We examined dyadic head-movement synchrony among 96 participants across 18 virtual robot-facilitated anxiety support group sessions. A human-controlled virtual robot, via a Wizard-of-Oz (WoZ) system, facilitated all sessions. We found that stronger peak synchrony predicted lower post-session negative affect. In contrast, speakers who more often followed listeners' movements reported higher negative affect and state anxiety, demonstrating that synchrony strength and direction capture distinct interpersonal processes. Participants who believed the robot was autonomous showed more genuine synchrony and stronger peaks than those who believed it was human-operated; more negative attitudes toward robots also predicted greater synchrony. These findings support synchrony as an objective, behaviorally grounded measure for evaluating robot-facilitated groups and a potential signal for guiding future autonomous facilitators.
